newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Corruption charges herald Kremlin infighting.
newsitem.headline: Corruption charges herald Kremlin infighting.

text.p: A new bout of infighting hit Boris Yeltsin's entourage on Monday, with ex-aides and officials trading corruption charges as the ailing president prepared for heart surgery.
Boris Fyodorov, former head of the National Sports Fund, accused Yeltsin's former confidant and head of presidential security Alexander Korzhakov of trying to extort $40 million from the Fund.

The timing of the charge, made in separate TV interviews on Sunday and Monday, suggested an attempt to block any alliance between Korzhakov, ousted by Yeltsin in June, and the ambitious General Alexander Lebed, who has his sights set on succeeding Yeltsin as president.
Fyodorov narrowly escaped an attempt to kill him in June and walks with a stick after being shot and stabbed outside his ostensibly well-guarded official residence.
Korzhakov, who blames Yeltsin's daughter and the new Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais for his sacking in June, could not be reached for comment. He is not charged with any offence.

The Sports Fund, described by Russian newspapers as an all-purpose Kremlin slush fund, used a lucrative tax break to import alcohol and tobacco free of duty, making huge profits. The money was supposed to go into developing Russian sport, but some sports administrators have complained that they have seen little cash.

NTV commercial television linked Fyodorov's accusation against Korzhakov with Lebed's need for political funding. The former paratroop general, now Yeltsin's security supremo, entered politics just a year ago but has open presidential ambitions and has irritated Kremlin insiders by grabbing headlines and openly criticising the government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
"On one side, Lebed has clear problems financing his political activity," NTV presenter Yevgeny Kiselyov said.
"On the other side, there is Korzhakov, who until very recently controlled, through his people, two very rich organisations...the National Sports Fund and (arms export agency) Rosvooruzhenye."
Korzhakov said last month Lebed would be the next president. The burly former bodyguard wants to run for parliament, possibly for the Tula seat Lebed had to resign after joining the Kremlin.
Lebed has spoken up in defence of Korzhakov.

Adding to the atmosphere of intrigue, ORT television said on Saturday that Shamil Tarpishchev, the man who effectively controls Russian sports and the Sports Fund, had been sacked after unspecified "scandals".

Tarpishchev is a former tennis professional who rose to power and membership of the august International Olympic Committee through his friendship with his tennis pupil, Boris Yeltsin. He is a close ally of Korzhakov.
But Tarpishchev's deputy at the State Committee on Sport and Tourism -- effectively the sports ministry -- told Reuters on Monday he was still in his post, though unavailable for comment.

In a direct attack on Lebed on Monday, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, whom Lebed demanded should be sacked last August, repeated his attacks on the peace deal Lebed reached in Chechnya. Lebed was in Brussels, visiting NATO headquarters.
